The problem: a test rig replays route codes recorded from a fleet trial. Each code is a nonempty string of at most 12 lowercase letters, and there are at most 2000 of them. Two codes are equivalent when one is a rearrangement of the other's letters, using every letter exactly as often as the other does. Write
, which groups the positions of equivalent codes together. Within a group, list the positions in increasing order; order the groups by the position at which each group's first member appears.
, and an empty input gives no groups at all. Take
, and state the time and space.

: a key that every member of a group shares, looked up in a hash map that remembers which group owns that key. The words that point to it are "rearrangement of the other's letters", which is anagram by another name, and "at most 12 letters", which rules out anything that needs the letters kept in order. Sorting a code's letters gives a key that every one of its rearrangements produces too, so a code is looked up by its sorted form rather than by itself:
Sorting every code costs O(L log L) for a code of length L, so the whole run is O(N · L log L) for N codes, and O(N · L) space for the keys and the groups.

either inserts the position of a new group, when the key has not been seen, or leaves the existing entry alone and hands back where that group already lives, which is what lets one lookup do both jobs. The edge cases are an empty input, a single code, which is its own group of one, and codes that are all rearrangements of each other, which land in one group together.
The group order comes from scanning

once and recording each group's slot the first time its key appears, not from sorting the groups afterwards, which is the detail this version changes from the original: there the groups were sorted to make the test stable, and here the input order does that job instead, so a solution that sorts the groups by their contents produces a different, still defensible order and should be judged on whether it states that choice, not marked down for it.

Take 40 minutes, same rules. A warehouse install logs which beacon ids can hear each other directly, as an edge list over beacons numbered 0 to n − 1. A link list may repeat a pair, or pair a beacon with itself, which links it to nothing new. Two beacons share a zone when a chain of direct links connects them. Write

, returning one struct with a zone id per beacon, the total number of zones, and the size of the largest zone. Number the zones 0 upward in the order their smallest beacon is reached, scanning beacons 0 upward, so the answer is the same on every run. Use no recursion: an install can have thousands of beacons wired in a single chain.
where beacon 6 has no link at all; zero beacons; one beacon; five beacons with no links; four beacons with the pair
; and four beacons wired in a cycle. State the time and the extra space in terms of n and the number of links m.

: build the adjacency list once, then sweep the beacons in order, flood-filling every unlabelled one into a fresh zone. The words that point to it are "share a zone" through "a chain of direct links", which is reachability rather than a direct link alone, and "thousands of beacons in a single chain", which rules out a recursive flood fill on a chain deep enough to overflow the stack. A link that repeats or points a beacon at itself has to be filtered on the way into the adjacency list, or it does no harm beyond a wasted visit, so it needs a decision either way, not silent trust in the input:

blocks.text:
mixed: zones 0 0 0 1 2 2 3, count 4, largest 3
no beacons: zones, count 0, largest 0
one beacon: zones 0, count 1, largest 1
no links: zones 0 1 2 3 4, count 5, largest 1
duplicate links: zones 0 0 1 1, count 2, largest 2
everyone linked: zones 0 0 0 0, count 1, largest 4

c.v: It is O(n + m) time, since every beacon is pushed and popped once and every link is looked at from both ends, and O(n + m) space for the adjacency list plus the explicit stack. The stack replaces the call stack a recursive flood fill would use, and it holds at most the beacons waiting to be visited, never more than n. The edge cases are zero beacons, an isolated beacon with no links, a beacon linked only to itself, and a repeated link, which the "duplicate links" case shows costs nothing beyond the wasted adjacency entries: beacon 0 and 1 still end up in one zone, not counted twice.

This re-solves the second version from

The words that point to it are "no relation between a node's id and the ids under it", which rules out the ordering trick a binary search tree would allow, and "deepest node that has both", which is a property assembled on the way back up a traversal rather than read off directly on the way down. A node that is

itself reports itself upward; a node whose two branches each report something different sits between the two and is the answer; a node whose only report comes from one side passes that report further up:

Checking that both ids are present costs two more passes over the tree, so the whole answer is O(n) time, for n nodes, and O(h) extra space for the recursion stack, for a tree of height h. The edge cases are an empty tree, an id missing from the tree, and a pair where one id is an ancestor of the other, such as

, where the answer is the ancestor itself rather than some node further up. Skipping the containment check and trusting that both ids are present would drop it to one traversal, which is a fair trade only when the caller already guarantees it, and the statement here does not.

Write down, for each problem, the pattern you named before coding, whether it matched the one this page names, the committed page and exercise it re-solves, your time against the 40 minutes, and your score out of 3. Add one line on what changed between your first attempt at the original problem and this one, whether the pattern came back on its own or you had to rebuild it from the words in the statement. You pass this set when you earned the first two points on all three problems. A problem where the pattern still would not come is not ready for a third attempt next week; it is ready for the theory step of its page, read again from the start.
